title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (N = 240 paired intents) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM compared with an LLM‑only pipeline. Tasks were drawn as 60% in‑distribution, 20% distribution‑shift, and 20% adversarial‑prompt, and the experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across paired arms). The guarded arm could invoke up to one validator‑triggered repair. All 240 paired tasks were scored safe under both arms: baseline_success_rate = 1.0 (240/240), guarded_success_rate = 1.0 (240/240); paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; exact McNemar p = 1.0). Deterministic reconciliation shows no repair was invoked because every shared initial generation passed the deterministic validator. We report the preregistered design, execution and analysis artifacts, explicitly state that preregistered sensitivity and reconciliation checks produced no exclusions or flags (see analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json and analysis/missingness_summary.csv), interpret the null result under shared_initial_candidate semantics, and give concrete design recommendations for future emulation‑grounded NetOps evaluations.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into concrete device configuration and to automate NetOps workflows. Execution‑grounded benchmarks that run agents in network emulators reveal planning and workflow failures not captured by static text metrics [1]. A common mitigation architecture is generate–validate–repair (GVR): LLM generation, deterministic validation, and, when needed, an LLM‑guided repair step [2,3]. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory, paired experiment to measure whether inserting a deterministic verifier into an LLM pipeline reduces unsafe configuration applications under emulation. Research question: Does a deterministic verifier (with up to one validator‑triggered repair) reduce the paired unsafe‑apply rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline when the same initial LLM candidate is shared across the paired arms? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired confirmatory study (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) executed on an emulation benchmark; (2) full archival of execution, per‑call traces, and analysis artifacts; and (3) a failure‑analytic interpretation of a null result together with concrete recommendations for future experimental designs.
sections.related_work: Recent work has developed closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded benchmarks for LLM agents in network configuration to surface multi‑step planning faults [1]. Literature on automated configuration and program repair documents generate‑and‑validate patterns and reports practical gains in constrained settings, while also noting remaining semantic gaps [2,4]. Surveys and position papers advocate tool augmentation, verifier gating, and uncertainty calibration to improve safety and operator trust, but stress that domain‑specific calibration and integrated verifier evaluation remain underdeveloped for production scale [3,5]. Our study implements a preregistered paired test of the GVR pattern in an emulation‑grounded setting, directly addressing an identified gap: measuring verifier impact under realistic task partitions including distribution shift and adversarial prompts.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute paired difference in unsafe‑apply rate). Design and sampling: N = 240 distinct tasks executed as paired episodes (baseline LLM‑only vs guarded GVR). Task composition: in‑distribution 60% (144), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial 20% (48). Paired/shared semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: one initial generation per task produced and reused across both arms; only validator‑triggered repair could create paired divergences. Model and adapter: a single hosted model declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" was used through the registered adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one repair per task. Planned budget and stopping: planned_episode_count = 480 (240 pairs × shared_initial semantics); maximum_model_calls = 480; adapter call contract limited initial generation to one shared call per task and up to one repair for guarded episodes. Scoring and analysis: episodes were deterministically executed in the emulator and scored safe (0) or unsafe (1) according to the deterministic validator and simulator checks. Primary analysis used the registered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor with paired bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) and an exact McNemar two‑sided test. Missingness and exclusions: preregistered rules excluded pairs flagged as 'possible false-safe' (verifier PASS with simulator unsafe outcome) from primary analysis and defined sensitivity analyses treating infra failures as unsafe. The analysis artifacts show that no exclusions or flags occurred; see analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json and analysis/missingness_summary.csv for deterministic reconciliation and missingness counts.
sections.results: Execution accounting: The run completed per plan: planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240, hosted_model_call_event_count = 240 (one shared initial generation per task). Primary binary outcomes: baseline_success_count = 240/240 (success rate 1.0), guarded_success_count = 240/240 (success rate 1.0). Paired contingency: n11 = 240, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (paired_contingency_table.csv). Point estimate and inference: paired difference = 0.00; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Repair and model‑call activity: no validator‑triggered repairs were applied in any guarded episode (repair_attempts = 0); total hosted model calls used = 240 (consistent with shared_initial semantics). Deterministic reconciliation: analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms complete_pair_count = 240 and provider_call_audit stage_counts {shared_initial_generation: 240}. Sensitivity and exclusion checks: preregistered sensitivity treatments (possible false‑safe inclusion and failure‑as‑unsafe) were executed per plan; analysis/contamination_summary.csv and analysis/missingness_summary.csv show no flagged or excluded pairs, so the primary analysis was unaffected by exclusions.
sections.discussion: Interpretation of the null outcome: The primary hypothesis (GVR reduces unsafe applies) is not supported by these data; the observed null is informative under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because the single shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator for every task, the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to differ from baseline: only validator‑failing initial candidates (or permitted repair‑induced divergences) can change paired outcomes under the executed semantics. Statistical consequence: with n10 = n01 = 0 there are no discordant pairs to drive a McNemar rejection; the degenerate bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00] and p = 1.0 reflect that fact (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Design implications and recommendations: (1) To empirically measure verifier benefit under paired designs, allow independent initial generation per arm or permit larger repair budgets so that generator variability can produce validator failures in at least one arm. (2) Increase adversary strength (adaptive adversaries beyond a single fixed seed) when evaluating guard efficacy against prompt injection. (3) Extend verifier semantic coverage (beyond workflow/syntactic checks) and instrument verifier false‑safe rates by cross‑comparing verifier PASS with independent simulator outcomes. (4) Report and analyze repair counts, model‑call budgets, and latency trade‑offs to capture operational costs of GVR. Threats to validity: internal validity is constrained by shared_initial_candidate semantics and a single hosted model; construct validity by finite deterministic_netops_validator_v5 coverage; external validity by an emulation corpus (NetConfArena‑style synthetic device images and parameterized tasks) and single‑model testing; conclusion validity is limited because observed baseline unsafe rate = 0 makes the preregistered primary hypothesis untestable in this run. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived to enable reanalysis under alternative semantics.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a generate–validate–repair pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Every paired episode was safe under both LLM‑only and guarded arms, producing a paired difference of 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Deterministic reconciliation confirms that no validator‑triggered repairs occurred because the single shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator for all tasks. The null result highlights an important experimental‑design point: under shared_initial_candidate semantics a verifier can only affect paired outcomes when initial candidates fail validation or when the design allows independent generation or larger repair budgets. We provide the preregistration, execution manifest, per‑call traces, and analysis artifacts to support follow‑up experiments that vary generation semantics, adversary strength, and verifier coverage.

disclosure_statement: Models and orchestration: The experiment used a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") via the registered adapter 'hosted_netops_gvr_v1'. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock; a human Research Director selected the broad topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the lock, and no manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred post‑lock. Immutable master prompt: the exact immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Reproducibility pointer: the archived execution manifest and full per‑call traces, task manifests, and analysis artifacts are available in the execution bundle (see execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/ for deterministic_reconciliation.json, paired_contingency_table.csv, and missingness/contamination summaries). This Disclosure purposely provides the mandatory master‑prompt locator and concise autonomy summary; detailed per‑call traces and artifact hashes are available in the archived manifest referenced above.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompt templates, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidates failing validation.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed attacker protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and verifier PASS vs simulator outcome mismatches were planned to be flagged and analyzed (none occurred in this run).
